Photograph: David Hockney/Christie’s David Hockney Rare sale of David Hockney painting of beloved dog Stanley could fetch £2.5m Exclusive: Dog Painting 17 is believed to be one of only six of works from Dog Series in private hands and first to be auctioned Mark Brown North of England correspondent Sat 26 Sep 2026 03.00 EDT Last modified on Sat 26 Sep 2026 03.01 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google David Hockney adored his dachshunds Stanley and Boodgie and let them run riot – so much so that after one had an accident in the LA home of the actor Dennis Hopper, the painter is said to have quipped: “It’ll be dry in the morning, luv, and you can just pick it up.” But Hockney did not just indulge his four-legged companions, he treated them as portrait subjects for a series of paintings, one of which is to be sold by Christie’s. The piece is the first from a series of dog paintings by Hockney, who died in June , ever to appear at auction. “This is such an exciting painting for us,” said Tessa Lord, Christie’s head of postwar and contemporary art. “The rarity is kind of extraordinary.” The painting is titled Dog Painting 17 and shows Hockney’s first dachshund, Stanley, curled up on a cushion, fast asleep. It has an estimate of £1.5m-£2.5m and is one of more than 40 works that Hockney painted in 1994-95 for his Dog Series. Stanley, named after Stan Laurel, was picked out as a puppy by Hockney in 1987 and followed him around constantly. Boodgie, more reserved, arrived later. View image in fullscreen Hockney holding one of his dachshunds in 1993. Photograph: Photo Researchers/Getty Images According to Hockney’s authorised biographer Christopher Simon Sykes , friends of the peripatetic Hockney were astonished he was getting a dog in the first place. But they soon saw how besotted he was. The feeling was mutual and the noisy dachshunds soon became an essential part of his busy friend- and visitor-filled life in his Hollywood Hills home on Montcalm Avenue . Sykes in his biography writes that Hockney was not bothered about house training, with one friend, Jonathon Brown, recalling how the dogs used to defecate in his shoes. On a visit by Hockney for dinner at Hopper’s Frank Gehry-designed house in Venice, LA, Boodgie left a “gift” in the middle of the floor. According to Brown, Hockney did retrospectively wag his finger, telling Boodgie “no, NO!”. Then, “as Hopper’s look of a chain-gang murderer increased in intensity, Hockney added: “Oah, it’ll be dry in the morning, luv, and you can just pick it up.” Hopper , the story goes, was left with two choices: silence or murder. “He chose silence, but he looked like murder.” skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to Art Weekly Your weekly art world round-up, sketching out all the biggest stories, scandals and exhibitions after newsletter promotion View image in fullscreen Hockney at his Los Angeles home in 1987. Photograph: Anthony Barboza/Getty Images Hockney embarked on his dog paintings when he needed some sunshine in his life. He had lost several friends to Aids and was devastated by the death of one of his closest, oldest friends, Henry Geldzahler, to pancreatic cancer. The artist told one journalist he wanted “desperately to paint something loving”. Lord said: “He felt such a loss of love, this was kind of a catharsis for him.” Christie’s believes there are only six of the dog paintings in private hands, with the others owned by the David Hockney Foundation. The seller of Dog Painting 17 bought it after the dog series went on display at the LA Louver gallery, a wildly popular show that Hockney said attracted 7,000 people in four days – many with their own dogs in tow. Lord said the painting displayed “incredible spontaneity” and “fluidity of brushstrokes, but it still feels richly textured. You’ve got this sort of mottling underneath the cushion and you’ve got that slight flick of the ear that really animates Stanley.” She said the painting shone light on an important chapter in the life of one of the greatest artists of the 20th and 21st century. “I love the fact that there is this kind of innocence to it but it is so much more than that. There’s a universality to it … it’s so much more than just a portrait of a dog.” The painting will be sold on 14 October during Frieze Week, and it will go on display – anyone can see it for free – at Christie’s in London from 8 October. Photograph: Steven Saphore/AAP New South Wales Man charged with murder over shooting death of boy, 12, in Sydney last month A 19-year-old man was arrested and charged at Silverwater correctional facility on Tuesday Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Guardian staff Tue 13 Oct 2026 17.09 EDT First published on Tue 13 Oct 2026 16.19 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A man has been charged with murder over the shooting death of a boy, 12, in Sydney’s north in September. Police were called to a unit in Norwest on 21 September 2026 after reports of a shooting. Officers found the boy had sustained a gunshot wound to his face and neck. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email NSW Ambulance paramedics treated the boy before he was taken to hospital in a critical condition. Police said nine other people who were in the home at the time of the alleged incident were not injured. Three men – all aged 18 – were arrested, with two released pending further inquiries. The third man was charged with concealing a serious indictable offence and remains before the courts. About 8pm on 24 September, police were informed that the boy had died and the investigation was taken over by the state’s homicide team. About noon yesterday, police arrested a 19-year-old man – who was an 18-year-old at the time of the incident – at Silverwater correctional facility and charged him with murder. Friends and family paid tribute to the boy, who was a member of Sydney’s Maronite community. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | When needed Sign up to Breaking News Australia Get the most important news as it breaks after newsletter promotion Det Supt Naomi Moore told reporters in late September that police were “aware” of the unit where the shooting had occurred and had “engaged with the occupants previously”. “This shooting at this stage does not appear to be linked directly to current conflicts however a number of individuals who were inside the unit at the time are well known to NSW police,” she said. The man will appear in court today.
